title: Paper Summary: Carbon Retention in Boreal Soils
intro: A plain-language summary of our recent study on how fungal networks hold carbon in boreal forest soils — what we asked, what we measured, and what it means.

add_paragraph.heading: The question
add_paragraph.text:
Boreal soils store more carbon per square metre than any other terrestrial ecosystem, yet the mechanisms that keep that carbon in place are still poorly resolved. Our study asked a narrow question: **does fungal network continuity predict how long fresh plant carbon stays in the mineral soil?**

We paired a four-year labelling experiment with a survey of 36 forest plots across two latitudes.

add_image.image_alt: Soil cores laid out on a bench after sampling
add_image.image_caption: Soil cores from the northern transect, sorted by depth before analysis.

add_focus_list.heading: Key findings
items_of_the_focus_list: Fungal continuity explained 41% of the variation in mineral-associated carbon.
Fresh carbon moved into stable pools fastest where fungal networks were undisturbed.
Tillage reduced retention within a single season; recovery took at least three.
The relationship held across both latitudes, but weakened in sandy soils.

add_table.table_caption: Sampling design across the two regions.

add_quote.text: The carbon was never really locked away — it was being held in place, season after season, by a network we could not see.
